content: Keratoconus is an ocular condition that affects approximately 1 in 2000 individuals. It is characterized by a progressive increase in the curvature of the cornea, leading to a decline in visual acuity and a subsequent negative impact on the patient’s quality of life. Collagen cross-linking (CXL) is a relatively novel therapeutic intervention that combines ultraviolet A (UVA) light with riboflavin (vitamin B2). This treatment has been reported to slow or halt the progression of keratoconus, particularly in its early stages. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether CXL is an effective and safe treatment for halting the progression of keratoconus when compared to no treatment. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, CINAHL, OpenGrey, mRCT, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, was conducted. The search included studies published up to August 28, 2014, without restrictions on language or publication date. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing CXL with no treatment in individuals with keratoconus were included in the analysis. Three RCTs conducted in Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States were included in the review. These trials collectively analyzed 219 eyes, with 119 eyes receiving CXL (using the epithelium-off technique) and 100 eyes serving as controls. The total number of participants was unclear in two of the studies, but all participants were adults. The studies were assessed to have a high risk of performance bias (due to lack of masking), detection bias (only one trial attempted to mask outcome assessment), and attrition bias (due to incomplete follow-up). Differences in outcome measurement and reporting precluded pooling of data across studies. Limited evidence was available regarding the risk of keratoconus progression. In one study, analysis of a small subset of participants followed for one year suggested that eyes treated with CXL were less likely to experience an increase in maximum keratometry of 1.5 diopters (D) or more compared to untreated eyes. However, the confidence intervals (CI) were wide, indicating uncertainty in the effect (risk ratio [RR] 0.12, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.00, 19 eyes). The same study reported that, at 36 months, the risk of an increase in keratometry of 2 D or more was lower in the CXL group (RR 0.03, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.43, 94 eyes). Another study, using a different definition of progression, found that at 18 months, individuals receiving CXL were less likely to progress, but the effect remained uncertain (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.61, 44 eyes). The quality of evidence was judged to be very low due to risks of bias, imprecision, indirectness, and potential publication bias, although the potential effect size was large. On average, eyes treated with CXL demonstrated a less steep cornea (approximately 2 D flatter) at 12 months compared to untreated eyes (mean difference [MD] -1.92, 95% CI -2.54 to -1.30, 94 eyes, 1 RCT, very low-quality evidence). Additionally, treated eyes exhibited better uncorrected visual acuity, with an improvement of approximately 2 lines or 10 letters on a visual acuity chart (MD -0.20, 95% CI -0.31 to -0.09, 94 eyes, 1 RCT, very low-quality evidence). None of the studies reported a loss of 0.2 logMAR acuity. Data on corneal thickness were inconsistent, and no data were available regarding quality of life or treatment costs. Adverse effects associated with CXL were not uncommon but were generally transient and of low clinical significance. In one trial, 3 out of 12 participants treated with CXL experienced adverse effects, including corneal edema, anterior chamber inflammation, and recurrent corneal erosions. In another trial, at 3 years, 3 out of 50 participants reported adverse events such as mild diffuse corneal edema, paracentral infiltrates, peripheral corneal vascularization, subepithelial infiltrates, and anterior chamber inflammation. No adverse effects were reported in the control groups. In conclusion, the evidence supporting the use of CXL for managing keratoconus is limited due to the lack of well-conducted RCTs. While some studies suggest that CXL may reduce the progression of keratoconus and improve corneal steepness and visual acuity, the quality of evidence is very low, and further high-quality research is needed to confirm these findings.
